A foregone conclusion is an outcome or result that is so certain and predictable that it feels like it has already been decided, even before it actually happens. There is no real suspense, no genuine doubt — everyone can see where things are heading, and the final result is basically a formality.

Think of it this way: if you watch a chess match where one player has already lost their queen, both rooks, and most of their pieces, the other player's victory is a foregone conclusion. The game isn't technically over yet, but the outcome is as good as sealed.

To truly understand this idiom, it helps to look at the two key words:

  • "Foregone" — This comes from the old verb forego, meaning "to go before" or "to precede." So "foregone" means "that which has already passed or been decided beforehand." (Be careful: this is different from "forgo," which means "to give something up." They look similar but mean completely different things.)
  • "Conclusion" — This simply means a result, decision, or ending.

Put them together: a foregone conclusion is literally "a result that has already been gone through beforehand" — in other words, a result that was decided before anyone even finished deliberating.

This phrase was invented by William Shakespeare in his famous tragedy Othello, written around 1603. In the play, the villain Iago manipulates Othello into believing his wife has been unfaithful, and Othello uses the phrase to refer to something that seems already confirmed in his mind.

Interestingly, Shakespeare's original usage had a slightly more specific meaning — referring to something that had literally been experienced or gone through in advance. Over the centuries, the phrase evolved into its modern, broader meaning: any outcome that seems inevitable or already decided.

The fact that this phrase has survived for over 400 years and is still used in everyday English today tells you how powerful and useful it is.

This idiom is not just about certainty — it also carries a particular emotional tone depending on the context:

  • Resignation — Sometimes people use it with a sense of "well, we already knew this would happen," as if the process in between was pointless.
  • Frustration or Sarcasm — If someone goes through a big show of pretending to deliberate when the decision was clearly already made, calling it "a foregone conclusion" can be a subtle way of pointing out that the whole process was fake or hollow.
  • Simple Confidence — Other times, it's used in a neutral or even positive way, simply to acknowledge that something is extremely likely.

The idiom itself is neither positive nor negative — the tone depends entirely on the situation.

Here are several examples across different areas of life, so you can see how naturally it fits into conversation:

Sports:

"Once their star striker got injured in the first half, the defeat was a foregone conclusion."

Politics:

"With such overwhelming support in the polls, her re-election was a foregone conclusion long before voting day."

Work/Business:

"After the audit revealed those financial irregularities, the CEO's resignation was a foregone conclusion."

Everyday life:

"He had been practicing piano for ten years, so winning the competition felt like a foregone conclusion to everyone who knew him."

Sarcastic use:

"They held a three-hour meeting to decide whether to keep their most profitable product. A foregone conclusion dressed up as a debate."

In every case, notice that the result was expected by everyone well in advance, and the eventual outcome simply confirmed what people already knew.
How Certain Does Something Have to Be?

This is an important nuance. A foregone conclusion does not just mean "something that is likely." It means something that is virtually certain — so predictable that calling it a surprise would be absurd. The doubt is basically zero, or close to it.

For example:

  • If your team has a 60% chance of winning a game → that is not a foregone conclusion.
  • If your team is playing against opponents who have already lost five players to injury and are down 5–0 in the last minute → that is a foregone conclusion.

The phrase implies that the outcome is already written, even if the last few formalities haven't played out yet.

Avoid confusing "a foregone conclusion" with these similar-sounding but different ideas:

  • "A lucky guess" — A foregone conclusion isn't a guess at all. It's a certainty backed by clear evidence or overwhelming circumstances.
  • "A self-fulfilling prophecy" — That's when your belief in an outcome causes it to happen. A foregone conclusion is simply one that was always going to happen, regardless of your belief.
  • "A snap judgment" — That's a quick decision made without much thought. A foregone conclusion is about a predictable outcome, not about how fast a decision is made.

These words and phrases carry a similar meaning and can sometimes be used in place of "a foregone conclusion":

  • A certainty — the outcome is sure
  • A done deal — it's already decided (slightly more informal)
  • Inevitable (adjective) — it cannot be avoided
  • A sure thing — informal; very likely to happen
  • Written in the stars — fate has already decided it
  • A no-brainer — so obvious there's nothing to think about (though this leans more toward easy decisions than certain outcomes)

ConceptDetail

"A foregone conclusion" means: the result was never really in doubt. It was predictable, obvious, and effectively decided before the process even finished. You use it when an outcome is so clear that going through the motions feels almost unnecessary. It's a phrase born from Shakespeare, refined over 400 years, and still alive and well in modern English — because the idea of an inevitable outcome is something every human being understands.
21: A fortiori is an adverb meaning "with even stronger reason" or "all the more so." You use it when a conclusion is even more obviously true than something you've already established. It says: if that first thing is true, this second thing follows — and it follows even more forcefully.

The heart of a fortiori reasoning is a comparison between two cases: a weaker/easier case and a stronger/harder case. The argument works like this:

If something holds true even in the less obvious case, then a fortiori — with even greater certainty — it must hold true in the more obvious case.

Imagine a bar that needs to be cleared. A fortiori says: "Look, the bar was already cleared in the harder situation. So obviously it's cleared in the easier one too — even more so."
The two directions it can work in

A fortiori reasoning works in both directions:

Direction 1 — From less extreme to more extreme (upward):
If something is wrong/true/possible in a lesser case, it is a fortiori wrong/true/possible in a greater case.

"If stealing a small amount is a crime, then a fortiori, stealing a large amount is a crime."

We start from the lesser wrong (small theft) and conclude with even greater certainty about the bigger wrong (large theft). The second conclusion doesn't even need to be argued — it follows so obviously.

Direction 2 — From more extreme to less extreme (downward):
If something is impossible/insufficient in a stronger case, it is a fortiori impossible/insufficient in the weaker case.

"If the strongest antibiotic cannot cure this infection, then a fortiori, a weaker antibiotic cannot cure it either."

Here, we establish that even the best option fails — so obviously a lesser option fails too. The conclusion is even more certain than the starting point.

Both directions share the same logic: the second conclusion requires even less justification than the first, because the first already did the heavy lifting.

Example 1:

"If a healthy, trained athlete cannot survive three weeks without food, then a fortiori, a sick and frail person cannot."

We know the stronger case (healthy athlete) fails. So the weaker case (sick person) fails even more obviously. A fortiori signals: "This doesn't even need arguing."

Example 2:

"The government couldn't manage a small housing project efficiently; a fortiori, it cannot be trusted to run an entire national infrastructure program."

Failure at the smaller scale is established. The larger scale failure follows with even greater certainty.

Example 3:

"If you cannot understand this chapter after reading it once, then a fortiori, a child encountering it for the first time cannot."

The harder case (adult rereading) is established. The easier-to-believe case (child, first time) follows even more obviously.

Example 4 (negative direction):

"She doesn't even have time for her closest friends; a fortiori, she has no time for acquaintances."

Not having time for the priority (close friends) implies she a fortiori doesn't have it for lesser priorities.

This is a subtle but important distinction.

  • "Therefore" simply means: this conclusion follows from what came before. It's about logical consequence.
  • "A fortiori" means: this conclusion follows from what came before with even greater force than what came before itself. It's about logical consequence that is even more compelling than the premise.

When you say a fortiori, you're doing something extra — you're claiming that the second conclusion is more obvious or more necessary than the first one you used to reach it. You're essentially saying: "And if you thought the first thing was clear, wait until you see how obvious this second thing is."

Think of it this way: "therefore" is a bridge. A fortiori is a bridge that slopes downhill — the conclusion is easier to reach than the starting point.

A fortiori appears most often in formal contexts: philosophy, law, academic writing, and careful intellectual argument. In courtrooms, lawyers use it constantly — "if the lesser offense is punishable, then a fortiori, the greater offense is punishable." In philosophy, it's used to extend an argument from a case that's been proven to one that needs even less proof.

In everyday speech, people say the same thing with phrases like "all the more so," "even more so," or "certainly then." A fortiori is just the precise, formal version of those.

Structurally, it usually appears between two clauses, connecting an already-established point to the stronger conclusion that follows from it. Sometimes it comes at the start of a sentence introducing that conclusion:

"The plan failed every small-scale test. A fortiori, it will fail at national scale."
The one thing that makes it tick

The whole power of a fortiori rests on a scale or degree relationship between the two cases. There must be a clear sense that one case is more or less than the other — more dangerous, more expensive, more difficult, more obvious — and the argument exploits that difference. If the two cases aren't on the same scale (stronger/weaker, more/less extreme), a fortiori doesn't apply.

This is what separates it from ordinary logical inference. It's not just "this follows from that." It's "this follows from that so obviously that it almost goes without saying — in fact, more obviously than the thing I used to get here."
**A fortiori means: "with even stronger reason" — used when a conclusion is so obviously implied by what you've already established that it needs even less argument than the starting point itself.*

"A hard nut to crack" means something that is very difficult to deal with, solve, or understand — or someone who is very difficult to know, persuade, or get along with.

In short, if something or someone is "a hard nut to crack," it takes a lot of effort, patience, and skill to handle them.
Where Does It Come From? (The Origin)

The idiom comes from something very real and physical — the act of cracking open a nut.

Think of a walnut or a hazelnut. The delicious part (the kernel) is locked inside a hard shell. Some nuts have shells so tough that you need a special tool, a lot of force, or serious patience just to get inside. The nut itself isn't the problem — it's getting through the hard shell to reach what's inside.

People noticed this and started using it as a metaphor for life's challenges:

Just like a nut with a tough shell, some problems and some people are hard to "get into" or "get through."

This expression has been used in the English language since at least the 17th century, making it a very old and well-established idiom. Variations of it appeared in English literature and writing from around the 1600s onward.
The Two Main Ways It Is Used

This idiom can refer to two things: a difficult situation/problem, or a difficult person.

1. A Difficult Problem or Situation

When you use this idiom for a problem, it means the problem is complex, tricky, or stubborn — it doesn't give up easily.

Examples:

  • "Reducing global poverty is a hard nut to crack."
  • "The last chapter of this physics textbook is a real hard nut to crack."
  • "Finding a cure for this disease has been a hard nut to crack for scientists."

2. A Difficult Person

When used for a person, it usually means the person is hard to understand, get close to, persuade, or communicate with. They may be emotionally closed off, very stubborn, or just complex in nature.

Examples:

  • "My new boss barely talks to anyone — he's a hard nut to crack."
  • "She doesn't open up easily. She's always been a hard nut to crack."
  • "The negotiator said the opposing team was a hard nut to crack."
Breaking Down the Grammar

"A hard nut to crack" is a noun phrase. This means it works like a noun in a sentence — it can be the subject, the object, or the complement.

  • As the subject: "This puzzle is a hard nut to crack."
  • As the object: "We knew we were dealing with a hard nut to crack."
  • After "be" (as a complement): "The question of climate policy is a hard nut to crack."

You'll almost always see the article "a" before it (not "the"), because it's used in a general sense.
Common Variations

The idiom also appears with the word "tough" instead of "hard":

"A tough nut to crack"

Both mean exactly the same thing. "Tough nut" is just as common, if not more common in some regions, especially in American English. You can use either one freely.
Tone and Register — When Can You Use It?

This is an informal to semi-formal idiom. You can comfortably use it in:

  • Everyday conversation with friends, family, or colleagues
  • Informal writing (emails, messages, blogs)
  • Journalism and news articles
  • Speeches and presentations

You would generally avoid it in highly formal academic writing or legal documents, where precise technical language is expected instead.
What It Does NOT Mean

A few things to be careful about:

  • It does not mean something is impossible — just difficult. Hard nuts can still be cracked. There's always hope.
  • It does not mean the person or problem is bad — just challenging. A hard nut to crack can still have something valuable inside, just like a real nut.
  • It is not an insult when used for a person. Calling someone "a hard nut to crack" is more of an observation about their complexity or reserved nature, not a criticism of their character.
The Opposite — Easy Things

If a "hard nut to crack" describes something difficult, then the opposite would be described with expressions like:

  • "A piece of cake" — something very easy
  • "A walk in the park" — effortless
  • "Child's play" — so simple, even a child could do it

For example: "I thought the exam would be a hard nut to crack, but it turned out to be a piece of cake."
Similar Expressions (Same Idea, Different Words)

If you want to say the same thing in a different way, you could use:

  • "A thorny issue" (for problems)
  • "A tough cookie" (for a strong, difficult person — though this leans more toward resilience)
  • "A tricky puzzle"
  • "An uphill battle"
  • "No easy task"
Quick Summary

MeaningSomething very hard to solve, or someone very hard to understand/persuade
Used forProblems, situations, and people
ToneInformal to semi-formal
Variation"A tough nut to crack" (identical meaning)
Key ideaDifficult, but not impossible
One Final Example to Tie It All Together

"Learning a new language as an adult is a hard nut to crack. The grammar rules, the pronunciation, the new vocabulary — it all takes tremendous effort. But once you crack it, the reward is absolutely worth it."

Notice how beautifully the idiom works here — it sets up the difficulty, and then the phrase "once you crack it" playfully extends the metaphor to show success at the end.

That's everything you need to know about "a hard nut to crack" — its meaning, origin, grammar, tone, usage, and more. You're now fully equipped to understand it whenever you read or hear it, and to use it correctly yourself.

Someone takes a deck of ordinary playing cards — thin, flimsy, paper cards — and starts building a structure with them. They lean two cards against each other to form a triangle, then carefully balance more cards on top, layer by layer, building upward. Slowly, a little "house" or tower takes shape.

It looks impressive. But here's the thing: the entire structure has no glue, no nails, no support. Everything is just leaning against everything else. One tiny mistake — a shaky hand, a slight breeze, someone bumping the table — and the whole thing collapses instantly and completely. Every single card falls. Nothing survives.

This image is the heart of the idiom.

When you call something "a house of cards," you mean that it is a plan, system, organization, argument, or situation that looks solid and structured on the outside, but is actually dangerously fragile underneath — held together by weak, unreliable, or false foundations. It will completely fall apart the moment it faces any serious pressure, challenge, or scrutiny.

The key ideas packed inside this idiom are:

1. False appearance of strength. A house of cards looks like a real structure. From a distance, it can seem impressive. Similarly, the thing you're describing seems to be working, or seems believable — but it is an illusion.

2. Deep, structural weakness. The problem is not minor. The weakness is not on the surface — it is in the very foundation and design of the thing. There is no part of it that is truly solid.

3. Total, sudden collapse. When a house of cards falls, it doesn't partly survive. It all comes down at once. This is why the idiom is used for things that don't just get damaged — they completely fall apart.

4. Everything depends on everything else. In a real house of cards, if you remove or disturb one card, others lose their support and fall too, which causes others to fall, and so on. This is called a cascade — a chain reaction of failure. The idiom captures this perfectly: when one weak part of the plan breaks, it brings down everything else connected to it.

People have been physically building houses out of playing cards for centuries — it became a popular pastime after playing cards spread widely through Europe in the 15th century.

The figurative (idiomatic) use of the phrase — applying it to real-life situations — goes back to at least the 17th century in English. One of the early recorded uses appeared around 1645, and writers like Jonathan Swift later used it as well. Over the centuries, it became firmly embedded in the English language because the image it creates is so vivid and universally understood. Everyone knows how fragile a house of cards is — so the moment you use this phrase, your listener immediately feels the fragility you're describing.

The phrase is now used in virtually every English-speaking country and has even inspired popular culture, including a famous political drama series named after it.
How to Use It: Grammar and Structure

"A house of cards" is a noun phrase. This means you use it the same way you'd use a noun — as the subject of a sentence, or after verbs like is, was, turned out to be, or build.

Here are the most natural ways to use it:

  • "Something IS a house of cards" → to describe what something currently is.
  • "Something turned out to be a house of cards" → to describe something that appeared solid but was later revealed to be fragile.
  • "Something was built on a house of cards" → to emphasize the weak foundation.
  • "The house of cards collapsed / came tumbling down" → to describe the moment of total failure.

Notice the verbs that pair naturally with this idiom: collapse, crumble, tumble down, come apart, fall. These all reinforce the image of a sudden, complete breakdown.

In business and finance:
"The startup looked like a billion-dollar success story, but it was a house of cards — the moment the investors stopped pouring in money, the whole company collapsed overnight."

In politics:
"The politician's reputation was a house of cards built entirely on lies. When one lie was exposed, everything else unraveled within days."

In a personal relationship:
"Their friendship was a house of cards. It had been built on one person always pretending to agree with the other. The first real disagreement shattered it completely."

In an argument or theory:
"The scientist's entire theory turned out to be a house of cards. When researchers found an error in his core data, every conclusion he had drawn from it fell apart."

In everyday conversation:
"Don't rely on that plan — it's a house of cards. The moment anything goes slightly wrong, the whole thing will fall through."
Important Nuances (the Fine Details That Matter)

1. The collapse is not just possible — it feels inevitable.
When you call something a house of cards, you're not just saying it could go wrong. You're saying it is bound to go wrong. There is a sense of doom built into the phrase — as if it's only a matter of time before it falls.

2. The weakness is usually hidden at first.
If something was obviously weak from the start and everyone knew it, you'd rarely call it a house of cards. The idiom works best when there was a pretense of stability — when it appeared solid. The phrase carries a hint of exposure: the truth is now being revealed.

3. It often implies poor judgment or even deception.
When you say someone "built a house of cards," you often imply that they either knew they were building on a shaky foundation and chose to ignore it, or that they were reckless or dishonest. It can be a criticism.

4. The scale can vary.
You can use this idiom for something as small as a personal excuse ("His alibi was a house of cards") or as large as an entire economy or government ("The whole financial system was a house of cards that collapsed in 2008").

Knowing related idioms helps you understand "a house of cards" more deeply by seeing what makes it unique.

  • "Built on sand" — Comes from the Bible; means something has a weak foundation. Similar to "a house of cards," but it focuses more on the foundation and less on the chain-reaction collapse.
  • "A castle in the air" — Means a plan or dream that is unrealistic and has no connection to reality. Related, but this is more about wishful thinking than hidden fragility.
  • "On thin ice" — Means someone is in a risky or dangerous situation. Similar danger, but this is more about the person's risky position, not the structure of a plan.
  • "A ticking time bomb" — Something that will definitely cause a serious problem in the future. Similar inevitability, but this focuses on eventual explosion, not collapse.
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

"A house of cards" = something that looks organized or stable, but is built on such a weak, fragile, or false foundation that even a small problem will cause it to completely and suddenly fall apart.

The next time you see a plan held together by assumptions, lies, or wishful thinking — a business built on fake numbers, an argument built on one bad fact, a relationship built on pretending — you'll know exactly what to call it.

It's a house of cards.

"A kick in the teeth" means a sudden, cruel disappointment or setback — especially one that feels deeply unfair, humiliating, or hurtful. It is something bad that happens to you at the worst possible time, or something that makes you feel disrespected after you have already made an effort or were in a vulnerable position.

Think about it physically for a second: if someone literally kicked you in the teeth, it would be a shocking, painful, and degrading blow — one that catches you off guard and leaves you stunned. The idiom carries all of that feeling, but emotionally and situationally rather than physically.
The Core Idea: More Than Just "Bad News"

This idiom is not used for everyday bad news. If it rains on your way to work, that is just bad luck — you would not call it "a kick in the teeth." The idiom is reserved for situations that feel particularly stinging, unfair, or demoralising.

There are usually two things present when this idiom fits best:

1. You were already in a difficult or hopeful position.
You were trying hard, waiting anxiously, or had already sacrificed something. Then the bad thing happened on top of that. This makes the blow feel much worse.

2. The setback feels insulting or humiliating, not just unfortunate.
It is not just that things went wrong — it is that things went wrong in a way that feels like a slap in the face. Someone dismissed your efforts. You were treated unfairly. The result feels disrespectful to you.
Real-Life Examples with Explanations

Example 1:
"I worked overtime for six months to save the company money, and then they made me redundant. It was a real kick in the teeth."

Here, the person gave extra effort and loyalty. Being fired — especially after working harder than expected — is not just disappointing. It feels like betrayal. The company took their effort and then discarded them anyway. That is the "kick in the teeth."

Example 2:
"After training for a year and qualifying for the finals, she got injured two days before the race. What a kick in the teeth."

She did everything right. A whole year of sacrifice and dedication. Then, right at the finish line — not because of poor performance, but due to sheer bad luck at the worst moment — it was taken from her. The cruelty of the timing makes it feel like a kick in the teeth.

Example 3:
"They didn't even bother to interview me for the promotion — they just gave it to someone from outside. That was a kick in the teeth after all the years I've put in."

The person expected to at least be considered. Being skipped over entirely, without even the courtesy of an interview, after years of loyalty, is humiliating. It sends the message: your effort didn't even warrant a conversation.

Example 4:
"The government raised fuel prices the same week they announced bonuses for MPs. A real kick in the teeth for ordinary working people."

Here, ordinary people are already struggling. To see those in power reward themselves while making life harder for others feels deeply insulting and unjust. The contrast — their suffering vs. the MPs' gain — is what gives it the "kick in the teeth" quality.
The Feeling Behind the Idiom

When something is "a kick in the teeth," the person experiencing it often feels a mix of:

  • Shock — they didn't see it coming, or couldn't believe it would happen this way
  • Hurt — genuine emotional pain
  • Anger — because it feels unfair
  • Humiliation — like their worth or effort was dismissed
  • Demoralisation — a loss of motivation or spirit

The idiom captures all of these feelings at once, which is why it is so widely used. It says more in five words than a long explanation could.
How It Is Used Grammatically

The most common structures you will see are:

  • "It was a kick in the teeth." (describing a past event)
  • "That felt like a kick in the teeth."
  • "What a kick in the teeth!" (exclamatory, expressing disbelief or outrage)
  • "A real kick in the teeth for..." (followed by who was affected)
  • "That was a bit of a kick in the teeth." (softened version, British English especially)

You will notice "a real kick in the teeth" and "a bit of a kick in the teeth" are both common. The first emphasises how bad it was; the second is a softer, more understated British way of saying the same thing.
Tone and Register: When and Where Is It Used?

This idiom is informal to semi-formal. You would comfortably hear or read it in:

  • Everyday conversation
  • Newspapers and news articles
  • Sports commentary
  • Political commentary
  • Social media and opinion pieces

You would probably avoid it in very formal writing like academic essays or legal documents — but in virtually all other contexts, it is perfectly appropriate.

It is also emotionally charged. When someone uses this phrase, they are not being neutral. They are expressing that something was wrong, unfair, or painful. It carries a sympathetic or outraged tone.
British vs. Global Usage

The idiom is especially common in British English, and you will hear it frequently in British newspapers, football commentary, and political speech. However, it is widely understood and used across all varieties of English — American, Australian, and others — without any confusion.
Similar Idioms (and How They Differ)

Understanding related idioms helps you see exactly what makes "a kick in the teeth" unique.

"A slap in the face" — very similar. This also means an insulting or humiliating blow. The difference is subtle: "a slap in the face" focuses more on the insult and disrespect, while "a kick in the teeth" often has a stronger sense of pain and demoralisation mixed with the humiliation. In practice, they are often interchangeable.

"Adding insult to injury" — this means making a bad situation even worse by adding an element of humiliation on top. It is similar in spirit but different in structure: "adding insult to injury" describes a process (something was already bad, then got worse), while "a kick in the teeth" describes the event itself.

"A bitter pill to swallow" — means something unpleasant you have to accept. It is less aggressive and less personal than "a kick in the teeth." A bitter pill is something you must reluctantly accept; a kick in the teeth is something done to you that feels cruel or unjust.

"A blow to..." — for example, "a blow to her confidence" or "a blow to the team." This is more neutral and less emotionally charged. A "blow" can be any significant setback; "a kick in the teeth" specifically carries the sense of unfairness, humiliation, or cruel timing.
What "A Kick in the Teeth" Is NOT Used For

To sharpen your understanding, here are situations where this idiom would not fit:

  • You expected bad news and received it → not a kick in the teeth (no element of shock or unfairness)
  • A minor inconvenience → too small
  • A natural disaster or impersonal misfortune with no human element → it can be used, but the idiom works best when there is a human dimension — someone who could or should have done better by you
  • Purely physical pain → the idiom is always used metaphorically in modern English
Quick Summary

Literal imageBeing kicked hard in the mouth — painful, sudden, degrading
Figurative meaningA deeply unfair, humiliating, or demoralising setback, especially one that feels cruel in its timing or context
Key emotional qualityShock + hurt + sense of injustice
RegisterInformal to semi-formal; appropriate in conversation, journalism, commentary
Most common inBritish English, but universal
One Final Way to Remember It

Imagine you have just run a long, exhausting race. You cross what you think is the finish line, and instead of a medal, someone kicks you in the teeth. You are already tired and vulnerable — and then this happens. That is the feeling this idiom captures every single time it is used.
25: "À la carte" describes a system where you select individual items from a list of separate options, with each item carrying its own separate price or value, rather than receiving a fixed, pre-packaged combination.
Understanding it through a restaurant (the clearest way)

Picture walking into a restaurant that gives you two choices for how to order.

In the first option, you pay a single fixed price, and the restaurant hands you a pre-decided set — a starter, a main course, and a dessert. You don't get to pick. You take the whole package as it is.

In the second option, there's a long list of dishes. Each dish has its own price printed next to it. You browse the list and pick exactly what you want — maybe just a main course, maybe two starters and no dessert, maybe everything on the list. Your bill is the sum of whatever you individually chose.

That second option is the à la carte system. The menu is called an à la carte menu, and the way of ordering is called ordering à la carte.
The two ideas always at the heart of this word

Whenever something is described as "à la carte," two things are always true. First, there is individual selection — you choose items one by one from a list, rather than accepting a pre-set bundle. Second, there is individual pricing — each item you pick carries its own separate cost or value, rather than everything being lumped into one fixed price.

Strip away the restaurant setting and those two ideas are what "à la carte" always means, no matter where you see it used.
How the word lives outside restaurants

This is where the word gets truly interesting, because today "à la carte" is used far beyond food. Any system that works like that restaurant menu — where you pick and pay for individual pieces instead of a fixed bundle — can be called à la carte.

A cable or streaming provider that lets you subscribe only to the specific channels you actually want, instead of forcing you to buy a full pre-packaged bundle of hundreds of channels, is offering à la carte television. A software company that lets you pay only for the individual features you need, rather than buying the entire software suite, is offering à la carte pricing. A university that allows students to register for single courses without committing to a full degree program is offering à la carte enrollment. A wedding photographer who prices photography, an album, and prints as three completely separate services rather than one fixed wedding package is operating on an à la carte model.

In every single one of these cases, the word is doing exactly the same job — pointing to a system built around individual choice and individual pricing.

When you call something "à la carte," you are signaling several things at once. You are signaling flexibility, because the person gets to decide what they want rather than accepting someone else's decision. You are signaling personalization, because different people can walk away with completely different combinations based on their own needs. You are signaling the absence of forced bundling, meaning nobody has to pay for or receive something they didn't ask for.

There is also one important trade-off that comes up frequently in the real world: à la carte options are often more expensive per individual item than if you had bought them as part of a bundle. This is because the provider charges a premium for the convenience and freedom of letting you choose. So while à la carte gives you more control, it does not always give you the cheapest total cost — especially if you end up choosing many items.
How it functions grammatically as an adjective

As an adjective, "à la carte" describes a noun. It can sit directly in front of the noun it modifies, as in "an à la carte menu" or "an à la carte service," or it can follow a linking verb and describe the subject of the sentence, as in "their pricing model is entirely à la carte" or "the options are à la carte." Both uses are equally correct and common.

If you had to capture the whole meaning in one line: something is "à la carte" when it lets you select and pay for individual items from a list, one by one, instead of taking a fixed, pre-packaged set.
26:
"A labor of love" describes work that someone does out of pure passion or deep personal care — not for money, not because they are forced to, but because they genuinely love doing it.

The word labor simply means hard work or effort. The word love here means a deep personal attachment, passion, or devotion. Put them together, and you get work that is driven entirely by the heart.

The key idea is this: the person doing the work is not doing it for a reward, a salary, or an obligation. They are doing it because it means something deeply personal to them. And because of that love, they are willing to put in enormous time, effort, and care — sometimes far more than the task requires — without expecting anything in return.

Imagine a retired teacher who spends three years writing a children's book — typing late at night, rewriting chapters dozens of times, paying for an artist out of her own pocket, not knowing if it will even sell. She does it because she loves storytelling and wants to inspire children. That book is a labor of love.

Now imagine a factory worker who assembles boxes eight hours a day only because he needs a paycheck. That is NOT a labor of love — it is just a job.

The difference is simple: a labor of love is powered by passion, not by obligation or money.
Where Did This Idiom Come From?

The phrase is very old and comes directly from the Bible. In the New Testament, in 1 Thessalonians 1:3, the apostle Paul praises his followers for their "labour of love" — meaning the selfless, devoted work they did for others out of faith and care, not for any personal gain.

The phrase traveled from religious writing into everyday English over the centuries. By the time it entered common modern use, it had broadened in meaning. Today, you don't need to be doing religious or charitable work for the phrase to apply. It simply refers to any task — creative, personal, or professional — that is done out of deep love and passion rather than duty.
The Grammar: How Is It Used?

"A labor of love" is a noun phrase. This means it functions like a noun — it can be the subject of a sentence or the object of a verb. You will most often see it used with verbs like is, was, became, call, or consider.

Here are the most natural grammatical patterns:

Something is a labor of love.
"This garden is a labor of love."

Something was a labor of love.
"Writing that novel was a labor of love."

Calling/describing something as a labor of love.
"She called the painting a labor of love."

Notice that you almost always use the article a before it. You say "a labor of love," not "labor of love" or "the labor of love" in most cases.

Here are examples across different situations so you can see how flexible this idiom is.

A filmmaker spends seven years making a documentary about his home village, spending his own savings and working weekends. When it finally premieres, a journalist writes: "This film is clearly a labor of love — every frame reflects the director's deep connection to his roots."

A grandmother hand-knits a sweater for her grandson, spending four months on it even though a store-bought one would cost far less. Her daughter says: "Mom, this is a labor of love. He will treasure it forever."

A software engineer builds a free app in his spare time to help blind people read restaurant menus. He earns nothing from it. A reviewer writes: "The app is a labor of love, and you can feel the care in every tiny detail."

A man restores an old vintage car in his garage for two years, buying parts piece by piece, watching tutorials, and working on it every weekend. He says: "It's been a labor of love. I could have bought a new car for what I've spent — but that's not the point."
What Makes This Idiom Especially Interesting

There are a few important nuances — small but important details — that make this idiom richer than its basic definition suggests.

The work is usually hard. This is important. If something is easy and fun, you wouldn't normally call it a labor of love. The word labor carries the weight of real effort, difficulty, and sacrifice. It is the combination of hardness and love that makes the phrase meaningful. If you love doing something AND it costs you enormous time and effort, that is the sweet spot where this idiom belongs.

It is always a compliment. When you call something a labor of love, you are expressing deep admiration for the person who created it. You are saying: "This person sacrificed time, money, and energy because they cared so deeply. That deserves respect." It is never sarcastic or negative.

The result is usually exceptional. Because the person doing the work cares so deeply, they tend to produce something of high quality. A labor of love often results in work that money alone could never buy — because no amount of payment can replicate genuine passion and care.

It often implies the person was underrewarded or unpaid. There is a gentle sense of sacrifice built into the phrase. The person may have even lost money or time doing this, but they didn't mind — because the love was the reward.
When to Use It and When NOT to Use It

Use it when:
someone works very hard on something purely because they care about it, not for payment or external pressure. It works for creative projects (books, art, music, films), personal projects (building a home, raising animals, restoring antiques), and even long-term community or charitable work.

Do NOT use it when:
the work is done primarily for money, obligation, or career advancement. If a lawyer works 80-hour weeks on a case because she is being paid a large fee, that is not a labor of love — that is professional dedication. The phrase loses its meaning if there is a clear external reward driving the effort.

Do NOT use it when:
the task is small, quick, or easy. You wouldn't say "I made toast this morning — it was a labor of love." The labor part must be real. There must be genuine sacrifice of time, effort, or resources.

While these are not the same as "a labor of love," they are closely related and help paint the full picture.

A passion project is something someone works on in their free time out of pure interest. It is the closest modern equivalent, though it is more casual and does not carry the same emphasis on sacrifice.

A calling refers to work that feels destined or deeply meaningful — often a career or life purpose. A teacher who feels teaching is her calling works with the same spirit as a labor of love, but the word calling has a broader, lifelong meaning.

Pet project is sometimes used similarly but more loosely. It can refer to a favorite project even without the element of hard sacrifice, so it is not an exact match.

The opposite of a labor of love is work done purely for obligation, survival, or money — with no personal connection. Common opposites in spirit include expressions like "just a paycheck," "drudgery" (meaning exhausting, joyless work), or doing something "as a means to an end" (doing it only to achieve something else, not for its own sake).

A labor of love = hard work done purely out of passion and deep personal care, with no expectation of money or reward in return.

Every time you see or hear this phrase, picture someone pouring their heart into something that matters deeply to them — not because they have to, but because they simply cannot help it. That is the soul of this beautiful idiom.
27:
This idiom means that a person cannot truly change their fundamental nature, character, or personality — especially their bad habits or negative traits.

Just like a real leopard is born with its spots and will always have them no matter what, a person who has certain deep-rooted qualities — especially negative ones — will always carry those qualities, no matter how much they claim they have changed.

Think of it this way: the spots are not something on top of the leopard's skin that can be washed off. They are part of the leopard. In the same way, certain qualities are believed to be built into a person — they are not just habits, they are who that person fundamentally is.

This idiom is very old. It comes from the Bible, specifically the Book of Jeremiah (13:23), which was written thousands of years ago. The verse asks: "Can a leopard change its spots?" — using this as an example to say that people who are used to doing wrong cannot simply decide to become good.

Over centuries, this phrase traveled from religious texts into everyday language, and today it is used all over the English-speaking world.

To fully appreciate the idiom, it helps to understand why a leopard is the perfect symbol here:

  • A leopard's spots are not a costume. They are not painted on. They are a permanent, biological part of the animal — present from birth to death.
  • No amount of washing, wishing, or effort can remove them.
  • The leopard has no control over them — it simply has them.

Now, apply this to a person:

  • Some people have deep character traits — dishonesty, selfishness, cruelty, laziness — that seem to be permanently wired into them.
  • Even if they promise to change, even if they try to change, their true nature eventually shows itself again.
  • Just like the leopard's spots — those traits always come back.
The Tone and Feeling of This Idiom

This idiom carries a skeptical and slightly pessimistic tone. When someone uses it, they are essentially saying:

"Don't believe this person has changed. History tells you who they really are. Their true nature will always come out."

It is not a hopeful idiom. It does not leave much room for the possibility of genuine personal transformation. It is the voice of a person who has seen someone behave badly before, watches that person promise to be different, and says — "I don't buy it."

This idiom is almost always used in situations where:

  1. Someone has a bad reputation or a history of negative behavior — lying, cheating, being unreliable, being aggressive, etc.
  2. That person claims they have changed or behaves well for a short period.
  3. Someone else is skeptical — they don't trust that the change is real or permanent.

It works as a warning from one person to another, or as an observation about someone's inevitable return to their old ways.

Here are some examples to see the idiom in action:

Example 1:

"My uncle promised he would stop gambling, but don't get your hopes up. A leopard can't change its spots."

→ Here, the speaker is warning someone not to trust the uncle's promise because his deep habit of gambling is seen as a permanent part of who he is.

Example 2:

"The politician was corrupt for years, and now he's suddenly acting honest during the election. A leopard can't change its spots."

→ The speaker is expressing doubt that the politician has truly become honest, believing his corrupt nature will eventually return.

Example 3:

"She was always rude and selfish when we were growing up together. Ten years later, she hasn't changed at all. A leopard really can't change its spots."

→ Here, the idiom is used after the person's true nature has already been confirmed again — not as a warning, but as a conclusion.

These are the subtle details that will help you use this idiom like a true English speaker:

1. It almost always refers to negative traits.
You would rarely hear someone say, "She's been generous her whole life — a leopard can't change its spots!" It doesn't work as well for positive traits. The idiom is built around the idea of bad behavior being permanent.

2. It is about deep character, not surface habits.
This idiom is not really about simple habits like biting your nails or forgetting to charge your phone. It's about core character traits — things like dishonesty, cruelty, greed, or selfishness. These are not habits; they are considered to be woven into the fabric of who a person is.

3. It often reflects the speaker's past experience with someone.
When someone uses this idiom, there is usually a reason behind it — they have seen this person's true nature before. It is not just a random insult; it is a conclusion drawn from experience.

4. It can be self-referential.
Sometimes people use it to talk about themselves, often with a tone of resignation or self-awareness. For example: "I've tried to be more patient, but honestly — a leopard can't change its spots."

5. It is debatable as a truth.
In real life, humans can and do change. This idiom represents one philosophical viewpoint — that deep character is fixed. But many people would argue against it. So when someone uses this idiom, they are expressing a personal belief or a cynical opinion, not stating a scientific fact.
Similar Idioms That Mean the Same Thing

Knowing the "family" of an idiom helps you understand it more deeply. Here are expressions that carry a very similar message:

  • "Old habits die hard" — Bad habits or patterns of behavior are very difficult to get rid of.
  • "You can't teach an old dog new tricks" — People who are set in their ways cannot easily learn new behaviors or change.
  • "Once a thief, always a thief" — A person who has done something wrong will always be that kind of person.
  • "The wolf in sheep's clothing" — A dangerous or bad person who is hiding their true nature behind a good appearance (related idea — the true nature is still there underneath).
When You Should NOT Use It

Avoid using this idiom in these situations:

  • When someone has genuinely changed and the evidence is clear. Using this idiom in that case would be unfair and incorrect.
  • For minor, fixable habits. If someone used to be late for meetings and is now always on time, this idiom is too strong.
  • In very formal writing (like academic essays or professional reports) without careful context — it's best suited for conversational or semi-formal use.
  • As a direct insult to someone's face — telling someone directly "You can't change, a leopard can't change its spots" is hurtful and aggressive.

If you had to remember just one thing:

"A leopard can't change its spots" = A person's true, deep character — especially bad traits — is permanent and will never really change, no matter what they say or promise.

That's the heart of it. Everything else is just depth and detail built around that core idea.

"A long shot" means something that has a very small chance of succeeding. It is an attempt, a hope, or a possibility that is unlikely — but not completely impossible.

When you call something "a long shot," you are saying:

  • The odds are against it.
  • Most people would expect it to fail.
  • Success would be surprising.

But here is the key: a long shot is still worth trying. It is not zero chance — it is just a low chance.

"Winning the lottery is a long shot, but people still buy tickets."

This idiom has two likely roots, and both involve the idea of physical distance.

1. Shooting (guns or arrows):
Imagine a soldier or a hunter firing at a target that is very far away. The farther the target, the harder it is to aim accurately, and the less likely the shot is to hit. This is a "long shot" — a shot taken from a long distance, with a low chance of hitting the mark. Over time, people started using this image to describe any attempt that is unlikely to succeed.

2. Horse racing:
In horse racing, each horse is given "odds" — numbers that show how likely it is to win. A horse with very low chances of winning is called a "long shot." If you bet on that horse and it wins, you get a huge payout — but most of the time, it loses. This use of the phrase became very popular in the 19th century and helped spread the idiom into everyday English.

Both origins share the same core idea: a difficult, unlikely, but not impossible attempt.

1. As a noun (the most common use)

Here, "a long shot" is a thing — a plan, a person, or an idea that is unlikely to succeed.

"Applying to Harvard is a long shot for most students."
"He's a long shot for the presidency, but his campaign is growing."
"It's a long shot, but let's try anyway."

Notice the tone: there is hope mixed with realism. You know the chances are slim, but you're not giving up.

2. "Not by a long shot" — meaning "not at all" or "far from it"

This is one of the most common phrases built from this idiom. When you say "not by a long shot," you are strongly saying that something is far from true, far from enough, or far from the mark.

Think of it this way: imagine an arrow fired at a target. If the arrow misses "by a long shot," it doesn't just barely miss — it misses by a huge distance. So "not by a long shot" means "not even close."

"Are you finished with your homework?" — "Not by a long shot." (meaning: I've barely started)
"Is this the best pizza in the city?" — "Not by a long shot." (meaning: it is nowhere near the best)
"Did the team play well?" — "Not by a long shot." (meaning: they played very poorly)

This phrase is used to strongly disagree or deny something, often with a bit of surprise or emphasis.

3. "By a long shot" — meaning "by a great margin" or "by far"

When used in a positive statement (without "not"), it means something is clearly the best, biggest, most, or greatest — by a lot. It emphasizes a large gap or difference.

"She is the most talented student in the class, by a long shot." (she is clearly far better than everyone else)
"This is the best film of the year, by a long shot." (no other film comes close)
"He is the fastest runner on the team, by a long shot." (there is no competition)
The Emotional Flavor of "A Long Shot"

This idiom carries a particular feeling with it. It is honest and hopeful at the same time. When someone says "it's a long shot," they are:

  • Being realistic — they are not pretending the chances are high.
  • Staying brave — they are not giving up either.
  • Preparing the listener — so that if it fails, it's not a shock.

This is why you often hear it paired with phrases like "but worth trying" or "but I'll go for it."

"Getting into that film school is a long shot for me, but I'm going to apply."
"It's a long shot, but we might just pull this off."

It is the language of people who understand the odds yet decide to try anyway. There is something admirable in that.

It is important to be clear about what this phrase does not mean:

  • It does not mean impossible. If something were impossible, you would say "there's no chance" or "it's out of the question." A long shot still has some chance.
  • It does not mean easy. The opposite of a long shot is a "sure thing" or a "safe bet" — something very likely to succeed.
  • It does not mean the person is foolish for trying. In fact, people admire those who take long shots — especially when they succeed.
Real-Life Situations Where You'd Use It

• Job hunting: "Applying to that company is a long shot — they rarely hire freshers — but I'll send my résumé."
  • Sports: "Our team is a long shot to win the tournament, but stranger things have happened."
  • Exams / competitions: "Topping the national exam is a long shot, but I'm going to give it everything I have."
  • Business: "Getting that big investor on board is a long shot, but one meeting could change everything."
  • Daily life: "Will the bus arrive on time in this traffic?" — "Not by a long shot."

PhraseMeaning

"A long shot" = something unlikely to succeed, but still possible and worth attempting.

"Not by a long shot" = not at all; not even close; far from it.

"By a long shot" = by a great margin; clearly the most or best.

The idiom comes from the world of shooting and horse racing, where a shot or a horse from far away — with low odds — still had a chance. Today, it lives in everyday English to describe any situation where hope survives against the odds.

The next time you face a challenge that seems unlikely but not impossible, you'll know exactly what to call it — and exactly how to say it.

When someone calls something "a moot point," they mean it is either:

  1. Open to debate — a question that reasonable people can argue about with no clear, settled answer, or
  2. No longer relevant — a question that has become pointless to discuss because circumstances have changed and the answer doesn't matter anymore.

Both meanings are correct. Which one a speaker intends depends on context and, interestingly, on where in the world they are. This is one of the most fascinating things about this idiom, and it's explained fully below.

The word moot is very old. It comes from the Old English word "gemōt," which meant a meeting or assembly — specifically, the kind of gathering where community members or leaders would come together to discuss and debate important matters like laws, disputes, or decisions.

In medieval England, a "moot hall" was a public building where people gathered to debate and decide things. The word simply meant a meeting for debate.

From this, "moot" as an adjective came to mean: open to debate, arguable, worth discussing.

A question was "moot" if it was still up in the air — unresolved and worth talking through.

This is the key that unlocks everything.

In law schools around the world — and especially in England — there is a long tradition called "moot court." In a moot court, law students argue imaginary, hypothetical legal cases. The cases are not real. No one will actually go to prison. No money will actually change hands. The whole exercise is for practice — to sharpen your arguing skills.

Because the cases in a moot court are hypothetical, the outcome of the argument has no real-world consequence. You can debate all day, but nothing actually changes in the real world.

This is the seed of the second meaning.

Over time — especially in American English — people began to reason: "If something is theoretical and has no real-world consequence, why bother arguing about it?" So the phrase started to shift. "A moot point" began to mean not just "a point open to debate" but "a point so hypothetical or irrelevant that debating it is a waste of time."
The Two Meanings Side by Side

Meaning 1: Open to Debate (The Original, Especially British Usage)

Here, "a moot point" means a topic that is genuinely debatable — one where smart, informed people can disagree and neither side is obviously wrong.

"Whether Shakespeare actually wrote all his plays himself is a moot point among literary scholars."

This means: Scholars genuinely disagree. It's an ongoing debate. There is no settled answer.

Meaning 2: No Longer Relevant (The Dominant Modern, Especially American Usage)

Here, "a moot point" means something has happened to make a question pointless. The circumstances changed, and now the answer doesn't matter anymore.

"Whether we should have taken the highway is a moot point now — we're already home."

This means: It doesn't matter anymore. Discussing it won't change anything. The situation resolved itself.

"The director quit before the board could fire him, making the debate about his performance a moot point."

This means: The question of whether to fire him became irrelevant the moment he quit on his own.
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Intended

Look at the context and the words around the phrase.

  • If someone says "that's a moot point" while waving the discussion away — dismissing it — they almost certainly mean irrelevant.
  • If someone says "it remains a moot point" or "it is still a moot point among experts," they almost certainly mean open to debate.

In everyday conversation today (especially in American English), the irrelevant meaning is far more common. If you use this phrase yourself in casual conversation, most people will understand you to mean "that doesn't matter anymore."
The Apparent Contradiction (And Why It's Not Confusing)

It might seem strange that one phrase means both "worth debating" and "not worth debating." But the logic is clean once you trace it:

  • Originally: moot = open to debate (from the old meeting/assembly meaning)
  • Moot court: debates hypothetical cases with no real consequence
  • If something has no real consequence → it's pointless to debate
  • Therefore: moot point = something not worth debating

The word traveled from "a topic actively being debated in a meeting" → "a theoretical topic in a practice court" → "something too theoretical or irrelevant to be worth debating."

Meaning: irrelevant

  • "We already signed the contract, so arguing about the price is a moot point."
  • "He failed three subjects, which makes the question of whether he should have transferred schools a moot point — he can't graduate either way."
  • "The event was cancelled due to rain, making all our planning for the outdoor setup a moot point."

Meaning: open to debate

  • "Whether a higher minimum wage helps or hurts the economy remains a moot point."
  • "What exactly causes dark matter is a moot point in physics — no one has proved it yet."

Many people mistakenly say "a mute point" instead of "a moot point." This is wrong. Mute means silent or unable to speak. The correct word is moot, rhyming with boot and root. The confusion happens simply because "moot" and "mute" sound similar.

"A moot point" is an idiom with roots in Old English meeting halls and law-school debate practice. It originally meant a point open to honest debate with no settled answer. Over time — because practice debates in a moot court have no real consequence — the phrase gained a second meaning: a point that no longer matters because circumstances have made it irrelevant. Today, the irrelevant meaning dominates everyday speech, especially in American English, while the open to debate meaning survives in academic and British usage. Context always makes it clear which meaning is intended, and the two meanings are really two sides of the same coin: both describe a question that, for one reason or another, you don't need to resolve right now.
